title: Abscisic Acid and Water-Stress Signaling
objective: Explain abscisic-acid synthesis, transport, guard-cell action, growth regulation, and stress memory without treating ABA as a direct measurement of drought severity.

terms.definition: Isoprenoid growth regulator central to seed maturation, stomatal control, and many stress responses.
Reduction in water availability caused by low water potential, including drought or salinity.
Change in water pressure or conductance transmitted through the plant.
Persistent physiological or molecular change affecting response after the original stress has ended.

coreScience: Abscisic acid (ABA) increases in many tissues during declining water status and can move through xylem, phloem, and local pathways. In guard cells, ABA signaling activates ion loss, reduces turgor, and promotes stomatal closure. It also changes gene expression, root and shoot growth, seed maturation, dormancy, and protective metabolism.

ABA is one component of drought response. Hydraulic changes can alter stomata rapidly; soil drying, roots, leaves, vapor-pressure demand, salinity, temperature, circadian timing, and prior exposure interact. Stomata can close before visible wilt, and reopening can lag after irrigation because hydraulic and biochemical recovery are incomplete.

Short, controlled water deficits can produce acclimation, but repeated stress also reduces leaf expansion, photosynthesis, root function, and reproductive growth. Calling stress 'beneficial' without a matched control, measured dose, recovery, yield, and quality endpoint hides the trade-off.
cultivationRelevance: Use substrate water content or mass, leaf temperature, turgor, gas exchange, and recovery time together. A calendar dryback does not define the plant's water status.
After a drought event, restore water without creating chronic saturation and continue monitoring. Visual recovery can precede recovery of stomatal conductance or growth.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Method, sensor/location, container mass or water content, irrigation, EC, and dry interval.
Air/leaf temperature, RH/VPD, PPFD, airflow, CO2, and time.
Leaf posture, turgor, stomatal conductance, leaf water potential if measured, and temperature.
Onset, duration, minimum water status, affected stage, and repeated-event history.
Rewatering method, recovery time, new growth, biomass, flower development, and abnormalities.

misconceptions: ABA means the plant is dying: ABA is a normal regulator whose amount and effects vary with tissue and context.
Visible wilt is the first drought signal: Hydraulic and stomatal responses often precede visible loss of turgor.
Every dryback improves quality: Stress can reduce growth and yield; claimed benefits require controlled evidence.
evidenceLimits: ABA concentration is rarely measured in cultivation and varies by tissue, time, extraction, and conjugation state. Physiological proxies do not uniquely identify ABA signaling.
